sections.title: NEW AMSTERDAM AGENDA
sections.subtitle: A path to an intelligent, caring city
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A starting point for the next 12 years

# New Amsterdam Agenda

*A path to an intelligent, caring city*

A vision for the transition from a knowledge economy to an intelligence economy, and what Amsterdam and the region can do to become strategically relevant again.

Written by and on behalf of a growing coalition of Amsterdam entrepreneurs, technologists, scientists and civic builders.

Developed through action roundtables, interviews, working sessions and a working conference.

**Ruben Nieuwenhuis**, co-authors **Barbara Baarsma**, **Marco van der Werf**, **Peter van Sabben**, **Stijn Grove**, **Jan Scheele**, reviewers **Cees Snoek**, **Deborah Nas**, **Sebastiaan Vaessen**, **Stephan van Dijk**, **Frans Nauta**, **Valerie Bos**, **Rick Pijpers**, **Franklin de Bekker**, **Patrick Leenheers**, **Ruben Brave**

With contributions from 100+ Amsterdam residents through action roundtables, interviews, working sessions and the working conference (listed in the Acknowledgements)

Version — May 2026

sections.title: READER’S GUIDE
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This essay has two layers.

The first layer is a vision. It describes a shift that goes beyond technology: the transition from a knowledge economy to an intelligence economy, what that means for Amsterdam, and why the city and region’s current stance is slowing that transition.

This layer runs (primarily) from the prologue through Chapter IV. It is intended for readers who want to follow the line of reasoning and understand why the urgency is real.

The second layer is an implementation logic. It describes the five pillars on which the intelligence economy rests, the Urban Tech Coalitions as an implementation instrument, the criteria projects must meet, and the societal dilemmas that will inevitably arise along the way and require dialogue.

This layer runs (primarily) from Chapter V through the epilogue. It is intended for those who want to build.

Readers who want to go straight to implementation should turn to Chapter V. Everything needed to assess, prioritise and organise is set out there.

Readers who want to follow the entire line of reasoning should begin with the prologue. Spinoza is the guide in the prologue and epilogue because the movement from passive to active, the creation of the capacity to act, and the shift from protecting to building form the foundation for everything that follows. Without that movement, the roadmap is an instrument without a purposeful mindset.

This document is not a final report. The essay describes the changing economy, the choices before us, and the city and region we want to be.

It is a starting point. And, emphatically, an invitation to contribute ideas, make course corrections and, above all, start building together again.

sections.title: PROLOGUE: SPINOZA AS A COMPASS

quote.text: Do not laugh, do not weep, do not curse, but understand.
quote.author: Spinoza, Tractatus Politicus

sections.bodyMarkdown:
On a summer morning in 1656, a young man walked along Amsterdam’s Jodenbreestraat. He was the son of a merchant, educated in the Torah and the philosophy of Descartes. That morning, he would walk through the neighbourhood as a member of his community for the last time. The ban pronounced against him was the harshest the Portuguese Jewish community had ever imposed. Its wording was merciless: no one was to approach him, speak to him, or read him.

Baruch Spinoza left Amsterdam. He rented a room outside the city, learned to grind lenses and began to write. His lenses—the finest of his time, so good that Christiaan Huygens praised them—made it possible to see beyond the reach of the naked eye. His philosophy did the same.

It made it possible to see the world as it truly was, not as fear or habit made it appear.

• • •

At that same moment, the city was at the height of its power.

The entrepôt system (*the system under which all the world’s goods were physically shipped through, stored and traded in Amsterdam*) was the most efficient trading system ever built. Spices from Asia, grain from the Baltic, wine from France: everything passed through Amsterdam. The city was the nerve centre of the global economy.

The entrepôt system worked well as long as Amsterdam was the logistics hub. When trade routes shifted, colonial power changed and capital moved to London, the system lost its core function.

While England built its *manufacturing economy* and the first outlines of the Industrial Revolution emerged, Amsterdam’s elite opted for tranquillity. Rather than investing the capital they had earned in new ventures at home, they lent it to others elsewhere. Living off investments yielded more than entrepreneurship. The mercantile spirit gave way to what a contemporary described as a stale, sated contentment.

• • •

Spinoza could have predicted it.

He distinguished between two kinds of *affects*: ways in which people and communities respond to change.

*Passive affects* arise when you are swept along by forces you do not understand. Distrust. An urge for self-preservation. Fear. They feel like caution, and sometimes have good reason to develop. But they become a weakness when they prevent us from acting together. You react to the world instead of shaping it.

*Active affects* arise when you gain a grasp of what influences you. Ambition. Resolve. Joy in acting together. They grow as you understand more of the world, of yourself, and of the forces in motion.

They are the foundation of what Spinoza called the *capacity to act*: the ability to shape the future actively rather than merely undergo it. Amsterdam’s eighteenth-century merchants lived in passive affects.

They watched the shift from the trading economy to a new economy unfold. But they did not understand it. And so they froze.

• • •

Amsterdam is once again at such a tipping point.

We are moving from a knowledge economy to an *intelligence economy*. This is not a technological upgrade. It is a shift many times more fundamental than the transition from the entrepôt system to the manufacturing economy at the time—and one unfolding ten times faster.

Once again, public debate is dominated by a stance that slows us down. Anxiety about technology. Distrust of entrepreneurs. A deep need for moral certainty before we move. Passive affects in modern dress. While others build.

This essay begins from a different stance. Not from techno-optimism or risk moralism.

But from understanding, the only starting point Spinoza recognised. His thinking about freedom as the capacity to act, power as collective strength, and cooperation as the architecture of a free state is not a historical curiosity.

It is a compass for our time.

• • •

sections.navLabel: I. THE INTELLIGENCE ECONOMY IS EMERGING
sections.title: I. THE INTELLIGENCE ECONOMY IS EMERGING
sections.subtitle: On the shift from knowledge to intelligence as a factor of production.
sections.bodyMarkdown:
And that shift begins with a single insight: we are not facing a technological upgrade, but the birth of a fundamentally different kind of economy.

We launched the New Amsterdam Agenda’s action roundtables and working conference because we wanted to offer an alternative to the defensive posture in public debate.

The vision: building the intelligence economy together.

• • •

### From knowledge to intelligence

Until now, value creation has revolved around the classic factors of production: labour, nature, land, capital, raw materials and knowledge.

A new factor has joined them: **artificial intelligence (AI)**.

Sometimes physical—think robots; sometimes digital—think large language models and agents: ‘digital colleagues’ capable of performing a series of tasks or even an entire process.

These artificial beings learn faster than we do, produce faster than we do and solve problems at a pace far beyond human scale. In doing so, they change not only processes but the very structure of the economy.

For the past several decades, our economies have revolved around knowledge. The Amsterdam region built a successful knowledge economy on that basis: strong universities, a highly educated workforce and a service sector that serves the world.

Knowledge as a factor of production is inexhaustible but slow. The knowledge exists, but its application is constrained by human capacity.

Knowledge scales by educating people. That takes years and costs an enormous amount.

That phase is drawing to a close. Not so much because knowledge no longer matters, but because a new factor of production—intelligence—has arrived and is changing everything.

Intelligence scales by adding computing power.

• • •

**The intelligence economy is an economy in which artificial intelligence, under human direction, acts as a new factor of production that converts tokens (AI’s unit of thought) into solutions to societal challenges, higher productivity and new value creation.**

• • •

Where the knowledge economy revolves around access to scarce knowledge, the **intelligence economy** revolves around the ability to activate and direct this intelligence. Digitally and physically.

This is no minor distinction. It leads to a fundamentally different economy.

In the knowledge economy, the bottleneck was: who has the knowledge?

In the intelligence economy, the bottleneck is: who has the computing power? The data? The energy? The talent to deploy intelligence?

The factors of production are shifting. The balance of power is shifting with them.

That calls not only for energy and technology, but also for rules, integrity and a society capable of distributing them fairly.

The intelligence economy cannot emerge within the structures of the knowledge economy. Not because those structures are bad—they have brought us fifty years of prosperity—but because this old structure was built around a scarcity that is disappearing.

The promise of post-scarcity offers a hopeful vision of the future.

### Early signs

This is not a future scenario. The intelligence economy is unfolding now.

Google DeepMind is working with Commonwealth Fusion Systems on a breakthrough in nuclear fusion. AI simulations run millions of miniature experiments to keep plasma stable, the kind of work that would take human researchers generations. *Clean, limitless energy is coming within reach.*

Google and Yale’s C2S-Scale model generated an entirely new hypothesis about cancer, which scientists subsequently confirmed in living cells. An AI that does not merely analyse, but discovers. *The beginning of a new generation of therapies.*

In Singapore, Sharp Robotics unveiled the SharpaWave: a robotic hand with 22 axes of motion and more than a thousand tactile sensors in each fingertip. *When robots become cheaper than the cheapest labour, manufacturing returns home: faster, cleaner and smarter.*

And it is happening here at home too, in Amsterdam and the Metropolitan Region.

**Monumental**, an Amsterdam robotics startup, builds autonomous electric robots that lay brickwork with millimetre precision on construction sites across the Netherlands. In a sector facing chronic shortages of skilled workers and rising costs, AI does not merely solve an economic problem; it makes building affordable homes possible again.

**Pacmed**, also from Amsterdam, brings AI to the intensive-care patient’s bedside. Its software compares a patient’s data in real time with tens of thousands of previous ICU admissions and predicts when the patient can safely be discharged. It is now used in several Dutch hospitals. In a healthcare system buckling under staff shortages, this is not a gadget but an answer.

**Dexter Energy**, founded in Amsterdam, uses AI-driven forecasts to optimise the trading and storage of renewable energy. Its platform helps energy companies turn the variability of solar and wind into reliable, affordable electricity. Precisely the link the energy transition needs.

These are not promises. These are facts.

We are already on the eve of the intelligence economy.

### Exponential speed

What makes this phase different from previous technological shifts is its speed. Not linear, but exponential.

Where the telephone took 75 years to reach 100 million users and the internet took 7 years, ChatGPT reached this milestone in just 2 months.

This transition is being driven by **six exponential accelerations**, all occurring simultaneously:

1. researchers themselves working and coding many times faster thanks to AI,
2. the expansion of ‘verification loops’ into ever more domains,
3. a tripling of computing capacity each year,
4. models using data with ever greater efficiency,
5. an enormous increase in user data that strengthens the training signal,
6. an explosion of capital and labour in the AI sector.

The result is astonishing. A few examples:

Processes that still took a year in 2025, such as learning solutions in game simulations, now take just three days.

The programming challenge has largely been ‘solved’. In 2026, 41% of all code is already AI-generated, and AI’s reliability in software navigation rose from 15% to 72% in 16 months.

Mathematics and scientific research are also accelerating enormously. Models such as Gemini 3 Deepthink now score 84.6% on the Arc AGI2 reasoning test, leaving the average human (60%) far behind. AI is now detecting subtle errors in scientific papers that human reviewers missed.

An estimated global productivity gain worth trillions of dollars and an economic impact **10 times greater and 10 times faster** than the Industrial Revolution.

Those who respond linearly to exponential change do not fall behind gradually. They lose touch altogether.

For public policy, this is a fundamental problem. Our institutions think in annual cycles, budgets and coalition agreements. Our institutions and their plans are still designed for the logic of the old knowledge economy.

AI technology now advances in weeks. Soon it will advance in days. Hours.

Network effects amplify this. Ecosystems are self-reinforcing: talent follows companies, companies follow capital, capital follows infrastructure and vision.

Those who participate build a lead. Those who arrive too late become less relevant within the network as a whole.

### Milestones

To understand where we stand, we must name what we are building.

Every leap in civilisation arose when one fundamental scarcity was overcome.

The **Scientific Revolution** was a struggle against ignorance. Its method: systematic experiment and evidence.

The **Industrial Revolution** was a struggle against physical limitation. Its engine: machines that surpassed human muscle power.

The **Digital Revolution** was a struggle against distance. Its instrument was the bit: information moving around the world at virtually no cost.

The **Intelligence Revolution** is a struggle against the scarcity of knowledge. Until now, complex problem-solving was limited by the number of experts we could educate, deploy and pay. Human knowledge was scarce.

The new instrument is the token: artificial cognition that turns intelligence into a scalable utility. Intelligence becomes reproducible. Distributable. Combinable.

And with that, the economic core shifts once again.

So we are not talking about better AI chatbots. We are talking about a shift in the scale at which human capabilities can be organised, augmented and deployed.

There are two milestones: AGI and ASI.

**Milestone 1: AGI (Artificial General Intelligence).** The point at which an AI system can function at the level of an average human expert across virtually all economically valuable tasks. It is expected to become widely accessible in the second half of this decade.

**Milestone 2: ASI (Artificial Super Intelligence).** The point at which systems perform orders of magnitude better than humans. This means computing power on the scale of 10 to the power of 26 floating-point operations. Systems that, during training, have processed more text, images and data than a human could read in a thousand lifetimes.

It is a redistribution of a fundamental factor of production.

Anyone who understands that attention and problem-solving capacity are now becoming scalable can see that the rules governing competition, education, public administration and entrepreneurship, among other things, are changing.

### New raw materials

Energy lies at the foundation of the intelligence economy.

Energy enables **computing power (compute)**.  
Computing power generates **intelligence**.  
Intelligence creates **solutions** and new productive capacity.  
And solutions are converted into **value** (economic and societal).

The intelligence economy’s value chain:

**Energy → computing power → intelligence (models + data) → solutions → value**

**Energy** is the (new) prerequisite. AI systems are hungry. Training large models consumes more energy than small cities use. Inference too—the day-to-day running of models in millions of applications—requires continuous computing power. Without sufficient, affordable (clean) energy, there can be no intelligence economy.

**Computing power** is the new steam. Those who own GPUs, build data centres and can supply energy for AI training and inference determine where intelligence is produced. Compute is not a technical detail. It is a strategic asset, as decisive as oil was in the twentieth century.

**Data** is the new raw material. Not raw data, which is abundant, but high-quality, domain-specific, well-labelled data. Data from hospitals, energy grids, ports and transport systems. Data that, combined with AI, yields concrete solutions to concrete problems.

**AI Access** is the new dividing line. In the knowledge economy, your diploma determined whether you could participate. In the intelligence economy, your access to AI tools, computing power and data determines whether you keep up or fall behind. AI literacy is becoming the new basic skill. Not only for programmers, but for everyone.

Welcome to the intelligence economy.

• • •

sections.title: II. AMSTERDAM IS LOSING GROUND

quote.text: If you have ten problems and you want to solve all ten at the same time, you have eleven problems.
quote.author: Eberhard van der Laan

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Amsterdam, our city. We see you struggling. These paragraphs are an attempt to hold up a mirror. We are giving you some tough love. Because you can take it—and use it to grow.

• • •

### The decline

Dealroom recently published [data](https://dealroom.co) on the state of Amsterdam’s tech & AI ecosystem. The gut feeling is borne out by hard numbers.

Amsterdam now ranks #8. It first fell out of the top 3, then from fourth place, and now sits just below Zurich.

![Amsterdam AI startup ecosystem](/assets/01amsterdamAI.png)

And in the annual Enterprise Value Growth data, it ranks as low as 21st. Just above Moscow, just below Dublin.

![European Cities Gaining Momentum](/assets/02euc.png)

We are barely growing as a tech & AI ecosystem.

Amsterdam-based technology companies invest substantially less in capital and research than their European and American competitors.

Over little more than a decade, the gap has grown to billions of euros a year. That shortfall translates directly into fewer scalable companies, less control over technology and less economic dynamism.

Entrepreneurs and investors report that Amsterdam is losing ground as a location for technology-driven companies to establish themselves and grow. Not through a lack of talent, ideas or capital, but because of slow decision-making, fragmented policy and a growing regulatory burden that impedes scale and speed.

While other ecosystems make a concerted effort to experiment and scale up, Amsterdam remains mired in caution and fragmentation.

Eighth place is not the problem. Losing strategic relevance is—the seat at the table where decisions about standards and values are made.

### The eleventh problem

Amsterdam is struggling with ‘the eleventh problem’: trying to cover everything at once, which prevents innovation from getting off the ground.

What is intended to ensure due care translates in practice all too often into slowness, unpredictability and deferred investment. Permit procedures that take years, rules that contradict one another, and policy focused chiefly on enforcement rather than facilitation.

It undermines the confidence and pace needed to build. And the conditions for growth are deteriorating precisely in highly productive sectors.

This is understandable, because public debate and policy regularly reduce fast-growing businesses and technology to three frames: *moral threat*, *distrust of entrepreneurship* and *normative delay*, in which consensus becomes a prerequisite for progress.

**The moral-threat frame.** From a classically moralistic perspective, technology is portrayed as displacing an order founded on law, responsibility and human dignity. The underlying conviction is that freedom is fragile, and technology makes it more fragile still. Technology appears as a threat, hardly ever as a tool.

**The zero-sum frame.** Here, distrust of the tech entrepreneur prevails. Sometimes deserved as a corrective mechanism—we know of cases in which public values have been undermined. But applied too broadly, the assumption becomes that commercial success and social commitment are mutually exclusive by definition. When entrepreneurs help draft a vision, it is immediately cast as suspicious: ‘preaching to the converted’.

**The normative-delay frame.** This perspective comes with the implicit assumption that society first needs a fully crystallised moral consensus before we can build. The result is normative delay: acting only after every question has been answered.

These frames reinforce a reflex of distrust, at the very moment when cooperation and shared responsibility are needed.

### Patterns holding us back

The ground we have lost is therefore no accident. In interviews, action roundtables and the working conference, the following structural patterns were repeatedly cited as impediments to progress in the Amsterdam region’s tech and AI ecosystem:

**Mindset: a dominant protection mode.** The prevailing reflex is distrust, fear and protection. Technology and entrepreneurship are approached primarily in terms of risk. This leads to the eleventh problem: trying to cover everything at once, with rules and delays that gradually erode our collective capacity to act.

**Fragmentation: disjointed efforts with no scope for action.** The current landscape is characterised by isolated initiatives, fragmented programmes and limited cohesion. Government often operates passively and normatively. What is missing is an organised scope for action—a vision—embraced widely across society.

**Conditions: uncertainty and ad hoc policy.** The conditions for growth are not sufficiently in place. Policy responses are often ad hoc, come too late, and lack clear priorities and choices. The result is uncertainty for entrepreneurs, investors and organisations seeking to scale.

• • •

> **Amsterdam faces a choice: do we remain stuck in this protection mode, or switch to discovery mode?**

The age of ‘the self-celebrating crowd’ is over. We need to get to work—and work hard.

sections.navLabel: III. THE PROMISE: WHAT THE INTELLIGENT CITY DELIVERS
sections.title: III. THE PROMISE: WHAT THE INTELLIGENT CITY DELIVERS
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Amsterdam can once again become a city that looks ahead.

Less 'shouting louder', more ‘building better’.

The next phase of growth is not only about AI startups or the tech ecosystem. Above all it is about what technology makes possible for everyone: higher productivity, better care, smarter mobility, lower administrative burdens, fairer opportunities for work, and a government that acts quickly, humanely and in service of people.

*The mission: to build our way to the intelligent, caring city with the capacity to act restored*

• • •

### Better public systems

An intelligent city is a city that works better for its residents.

Less friction, less needless complexity, and faster, more human public services.

Imagine:

1. AI-driven soil measurements and risk models that predict and prevent foundation damage to homes.
2. AI-driven route planning that predicts how full waste containers are and optimises recycling flows.
3. Capacity planning in neighbourhood care that eases staff shortages.
4. Smarter traffic flows that make the city cleaner and quieter.
5. Predictive maintenance of bridges, quay walls and sewers that saves millions.

These are not distant visions. This is technology that will be available soon.

The question is whether Amsterdam dares to apply it. Whether it will designate sandboxes. Whether it is willing to put the preconditions in place. A city that organises itself around entrepreneurship and solutions once again.

The logical response to entrepreneurs who come forward with such solutions should be: *“Go for it, what do you need?”* Not a brake based on rules, but an acceleration based on trust.

### Fair chances for everyone

The transition to an intelligence economy must not create a new divide. That is why the New Amsterdam Agenda explicitly opts for broad participation across society.

AI literacy is treated as a basic skill, comparable to language and arithmetic. Not only for the highly educated or for technology professionals, but for pupils, working people, entrepreneurs, public professionals and vulnerable groups.

We focus above all on the opportunities for every citizen, rather than mainly on the downside of technology.

By investing in comprehensible technology, accessible learning environments and practical application in neighbourhoods and organisations, a new route upwards opens up instead of a new dividing line.

In this way technological progress is tied to social cohesion and economic independence.

The future is already here; let us make sure it is evenly distributed as well.

### New broad prosperity

Real equality of opportunity and inclusion do not arise from the redistribution of existing value alone, but from the creation of new value.

New broad prosperity.

The intelligence economy offers that possibility, provided we invest in infrastructure, entrepreneurship, access to technology and skills.

Most prosperity comes from doing new, previously unimaginable things. That is precisely where the power of AI lies, provided we let AI be more than automation.

New companies are indispensable in this. They focus on building new products and solutions, not on optimising existing processes.

Tech ecosystem development goes hand in hand with social development. The former needs more attention than it currently gets.

When Amsterdam directs the city's intelligence at concrete problems, the result is *new broad prosperity* that residents, businesses, civil-society organisations and the region can feel.

Then Amsterdam grows into more than an intelligent city: **an intelligent, caring city**.

### Sovereignty: by looking ahead and reasoning backwards

We already know a great deal.

We know that in twelve years' time robots will carry out a large share of last mile delivery.  
The question is who designs them.  
Do we wait until Chinese suppliers offer them tested and ready-made?  
Or do we build an Amsterdam coalition around Physical AI in logistics and public space now?

We know that urban decision-making is increasingly supported by AI.  
For mobility, for energy, for safety.  
Do we wait until American platforms deliver those systems as a black box?  
Or do we organise a coalition now that designs, tests and governs them together on the basis of public values?

We know that work is changing.  
That virtually everyone will need new skills in order to work with AI.  
Do we wait until unrest sets in and people begin to fall by the wayside?  
Or do we start building an AI reskilling coalition of education, employers, employees and government right now?

We need **future coalitions**!

That is how we become sovereign.

Not by taking the measure of others. But by building ambitiously together. By (learning to) collaborate at scale again.

• • •

> **"Amsterdam does not have to be a spectator of the intelligence economy. We can become a co-architect!"**

sections.navLabel: IV. MENTAL MODELS FOR THIS NEW ERA
sections.title: IV. MENTAL MODELS FOR THIS NEW ERA

quote.text: One of humanity's greatest mistakes is wanting to be right rather than wanting to be effective
quote.author: Stephen Fry

sections.bodyMarkdown:
On the attitude Amsterdam needs.

And on the mental shift from protecting to building, from fixing to designing, from choosing between extremes to the ability to hold on to both.

• • •

### Fixers and builders

Amsterdam is at a tipping point. After years of fixing and controlling, the energy to build the future of our city again is growing.

The classic opposition of left versus right no longer offers any grip.

The truth does not lie in the middle, but in the future.

The new distinction is: fixers and builders.  
*Fixers* repair and optimise what is already there.  
*Builders* create what does not yet exist.

Both are needed, but without *builders in a central role* the city cannot draw on its full vitality.

Politically that means a shift from the question 'how do we divide the pie today?' to 'how do we grow the pie for tomorrow?'

With entrepreneurs, technologists, designers and innovators, prosperity grows.  
With new value, lasting social justice becomes possible.

### Agency

In recent years compassion has strongly set the tone in Amsterdam. Care, protection and repair took centre stage. That is understandable and valuable, but it has also brought a one-sidedness. It is time to restore that balance.

What faded into the background was the fire to build. And the fire of our curiosity has had to make way for moral purism.

What disappeared along with it was agency: the capacity to actively shape the future instead of merely undergoing it.

These fires are precisely what is essential. They are the power to create what does not yet exist, to be enterprising, to innovate and to get ahead.

Generations of Amsterdammers shaped the city through that fire. And yet entrepreneurship gradually became detached from the moral story of the city. Builders kept building, often against the current, but felt less and less seen.

That is why a recalibration is needed. Not by replacing the values, but by bringing them back into balance, and in doing so reclaiming our agency as a city.

### Values

In 1947 Amsterdam received the honorary motto *valiant, steadfast, compassionate*. Words that describe a city that dares to act, holds its course and at the same time cares for its people.

It is time to put valiant back in the light.

Values form the invisible infrastructure of how a city decides, builds and lives together.

*Valiant* is the fire to create and to take risks.  
*Steadfast* is the ability to hold course, even when it chafes.  
*Compassionate* is the gentleness that strengthens and shares, without paralysing.

Together they form (once again) the anchor of the New Amsterdam Agenda.

With these values we turn tough love into aspiration and collaboration.

### (High Performance) culture

We have worked so hard at preventing the crossing of boundaries that we have forgotten what pushing boundaries looks like.

We have the knowledge infrastructure, the talent, the geographic position, the trading spirit. And we have the culture in-house to make all of it pay off.

A *high performance culture* is within reach. And the good news: the conversation about it is under way again.

The question is not whether we can build that culture, but:

> **How do we create a High Performance Culture in Amsterdam again (without becoming transgressive)?**

A profile of high performance that has nothing to do with toxic workloads or ruthless competition.

But:

**Psychological safety combined with high standards.** We are allowed to experiment, to make mistakes, to be honest. But the expectation of excellence is not up for debate. You are not punished for failing. You are punished for not trying.

**Ownership.** We take responsibility for outcomes, not only for effort. Working hard is not the same as delivering results. In a high performance culture you are allowed to say that out loud.

**Radical honesty.** Feedback is direct, specific and aimed at growth. Not wrapped in compliments. Not saved up for the annual review. But also not personal or destructive. It is a skill, not a character trait.

**Meritocratic recognition.** The best ideas win, but let us make sure they can come from anyone. Too often ideas are lost for want of a network, capital or visibility. That requires active investment. Achievement is acknowledged.

**A shared, ambitious goal.** Teams know what they are working for. That goal is bigger than the individual and bigger than the quarter.

**Room for constructive friction.** Substantive conflict is not merely tolerated, it is expected. Groupthink is the enemy. Combustible impatience is not a bug, it is a feature. Provided it is aimed at the problem, not at the person.

We want to build in a culture of performance.

### Vertical maturity

The turning point we face cannot be resolved by choosing one side.

It calls for vertical maturity: the ability to hold two truths at once, the skill of systems thinking and long-term thinking. Being interdependent.

Both progress and loss. Both opportunity and downside. Both speed and care.

Whoever recognises only one truth impoverishes the debate. Whoever holds on to both can design.

• • •

These mental models are not abstractions. They determine how we will make choices about infrastructure, talent, collaboration and trust.

They form the attitude with which we approach the five pillars of the intelligence economy.

sections.navLabel: V. THE FIVE PILLARS OF THE INTELLIGENCE ECONOMY
sections.title: V. THE FIVE PILLARS OF THE INTELLIGENCE ECONOMY

quote.text: When that happens, we need to have conversations about how we organize our economy. About how humans find meaning. There are a lot of assumptions we made, when humans were the most intelligent species on the planet, that are going to be invalidated.
quote.author: Dario Amodei

sections.bodyMarkdown:
You do not build an intelligence economy by doing one thing well. You build it by doing five things at once. And by understanding how they need one another.

This chapter describes the architecture. As a system of five pillars that each stand on their own, but only work when they function together.

The question this chapter answers is: how does an intelligence economy work, and what are the conditions under which it can flourish?

### Architecture

Our current economic infrastructure is built on the logic of the knowledge economy: schools that transmit knowledge, companies that bring knowledge to market, and governments that make policy on the basis of information.

But the rules of the game are changing.

In the coming decades we will have to redesign our economic infrastructure: from knowledge systems to intelligence systems.

Every link in this new chain depends on the previous one. Without energy, no computing power. Without computing power, no intelligence at scale. Without access to that intelligence, no solutions. And without trust — in the technology, in the institutions, in one another — no social value.

But this system also contains tensions. Whoever controls energy and computing power gains power. Whoever has less of it becomes dependent. Without ethics, transparency and fair distribution, abundance can tip over into inequality.

The intelligence economy is therefore not a neutral system but a moral question in economic form: who gets to compute, and in whose interest?

In short, we need something to hold on to: what are the economic and moral pillars we are going to build on? What are the pillars around which we activate projects, connect stakeholders and deploy resources?

The five pillars are the answer to that question. Together they form the architecture of an intelligence economy that is not only efficient, but also just, sovereign and human:

1. **Energy and computing power, as fuel**  
2. **Data and access to AI, for everyone**  
3. **Entrepreneurship and talent, the engine**  
4. **Compass and Laboratories, as direction**  
5. **Trust infrastructure, the societal foundation**

They are the pillars of a new economic ecosystem in which thinking capacity is literally powered by electricity. Where human creativity and machine computation flow together into a new factor of production: directed intelligence.

### Pillar 1: Energy and Computing Power, as Fuel

The fuel of the intelligence economy.

Everything begins here.

An intelligence economy is physical. It demands electricity, chips, data centres, cooling, cables. Scaling intelligence means scaling computing power, and computing power needs energy. Large amounts of it, preferably clean and affordable.

This sounds like a technical detail. It is a strategic reality. Whoever controls computing power determines where intelligence is produced. In the intelligence economy, compute is what steam was in the Industrial Revolution and what the ports were in the trading economy: the physical base on which everything rests.

The core shift this pillar demands is therefore not technical but mental: to stop seeing computing power (data centres) and digital infrastructure as a by-product, a risk or a cost item. And to start treating them as a utility and a factor of production.

Without this pillar the other four are pie in the sky. You cannot share data if there is no infrastructure to process it. Entrepreneurship has no scale without compute. Experiments fail when computing power is missing. And trust in technology is hollow if that technology is produced elsewhere, under rules we did not write.

> **The core shift: no longer treating computing power and data centres as a by-product, an evil or a risk, but as a utility and a factor of production for the city.**

### Pillar 2: Data and Access to AI, for Everyone

Access to data, AI and thinking power must not be a privilege.

The first pillar makes intelligence possible. The second pillar determines who has access to it.

Data is the raw material of the intelligence economy. Not raw data, which is available in abundance. But high-quality, domain-specific, well-organised data: the data of hospitals, energy grids, traffic systems, schools, ports. Data that, combined with computing power and models, yields concrete solutions to concrete problems.

The danger of this pillar is concentration. If data stays locked inside organisations and access to AI tools remains reserved for those who can pay, a new dividing line emerges: no longer who holds the diploma, but who holds the data and the thinking power. An intelligence economy that does not actively remove this dividing line trades one inequality for another.

That is why this pillar is not only technical but also political. Access to AI must be treated like access to education: as a basic provision, not a privilege. That calls for shared data infrastructure, for AI literacy as a basic qualification, and for a government that uses its purchasing power to compel data sharing and to democratise access.

This pillar connects the first with the third: without access to data and AI, entrepreneurship has no level playing field. And without a level playing field you narrow the ecosystem down to a small elite.

### Pillar 3: Entrepreneurship and Talent, the Engine

The intelligence economy calls for entrepreneurship and talent that thinks, designs and builds with AI.

The first two pillars create the conditions. This pillar turns them into movement.

Intelligence economies run on people who dare to make something that does not yet exist. Entrepreneurs who build new products and services with AI. Researchers who push boundaries. Talented people who choose an ecosystem because it buzzes, challenges and offers scale. Students who do not only learn about the world but also shape it.

The mechanism of this pillar is the ecosystem. Ecosystems work through network effects: talent attracts companies, companies attract capital, capital attracts infrastructure, infrastructure attracts talent. Whoever is inside this flywheel builds a lead. Whoever stands outside it finds it ever harder to get in.

But ecosystems do not emerge by themselves. They require coordination, as connective tissue. The link between university and startup. Between scale-up and corporate. Between local innovation and international market. Without that coordination talent fragments, capital is cautious and knowledge stays locked in silos.

This pillar is also where the social dimension of the intelligence economy is felt most sharply. Because if the engine runs only for a small part of the population, it is not an engine but a machine that excludes. Reskilling, inclusion and broad access to the ecosystem are not side issues. They are the condition under which the engine can run at full throttle.

### Pillar 4: Compass and Laboratories, the Direction and Space to Experiment

The moral compass of system renewal: progress requires direction.

The first three pillars build capacity. This pillar asks the question: capacity for what? What do we want this intelligence to do? For whom is the computing done, and which problems deserve priority?

This is the pillar of the moral compass. But not in the sense of braking or banning. Precisely in the sense of designing. A compass gives direction; it does not bring things to a halt. And laboratories (sandboxes, living labs, experimental environments) are where direction is turned into learning. Where you can fail safely, iterate and improve before you go to scale.

Without this pillar two dangers loom. The first is technocracy: technology that sets its own agenda, without public values as a design requirement. The second is normative paralysis: so many ethical questions that nothing ever gets built. The compass navigates between the two: it calls for direction while the building goes on.

Because intelligence in this economy is not only computing power and knowledge. It is also moral intelligence: the ability to navigate clashing values, to treat experience at the edge of the system as design capacity, and to acknowledge progress and loss at the same time.

This pillar connects all the others. Energy and computing power need a compass to know what they are being deployed for. Data access needs direction to determine which data gets priority. Entrepreneurship needs room to experiment in order to learn. And trust (the fifth pillar) begins here: with transparency about what is being built and why.

### Pillar 5: Trust Infrastructure, the Societal Foundation

Rules of the game and infrastructure that create trust.

This is the pillar that carries all the other pillars.

Without trust, no data sharing. Without data sharing, no intelligence at scale. Without intelligence at scale, no solutions. Without solutions, no new value. The whole chain grinds to a halt when trust is missing: it is a structural condition.

Trust in an intelligence economy is manifold. It is the trust of citizens in technology: that systems are explainable, that they do not discriminate, that they work in the public interest. It is the trust of organisations in shared infrastructure: that data is safe, that the rules of the game are fair, that nobody bends those rules to suit themselves. And it is the trust of investors and entrepreneurs in government: that policy is predictable, that experiments are facilitated, that government is a partner and not an obstacle.

You build this trust with architecture. With systems that are transparent by design. With governance that gives citizens and professionals a voice. With public trust layers that institutionalise explainability. With a narrative that is honest about dilemmas and therefore credible about ambitions.

The paradox of this pillar is that it is the least visible and the most decisive. You only notice it when it is missing: then data sharing stops, adoption stalls, public support evaporates and the flywheel comes to a standstill.

This pillar therefore also addresses the change side of the shift to the intelligence economy.

> **The coming years are about something fundamental: Amsterdam's capacity, as a society, to generate and direct the available intelligence together**

• • •

The five pillars are not a list. They are a system with a direction.

Investing in energy and computing power makes data sharing meaningful. Data sharing democratises access and makes entrepreneurship at scale possible.

Entrepreneurship generates visible applications. Visible applications (provided they are built with a compass) build trust. And trust makes further investment in the infrastructure politically feasible and socially desirable.

That is the flywheel. Each pillar strengthens the next. And every choice within one pillar has consequences for all the others.

Whoever understands this system also understands what becomes possible when the pillars work together. A data centre with a compass becomes trust. Access with infrastructure becomes a real promise. Entrepreneurship with social legitimacy becomes a durable engine. And trust with action becomes the foundation on which everything rests.

The intelligence economy calls for systemic thinking. Not everything at once, that is the eleventh problem. But always from an understanding of the whole.

Around each of these pillars, Amsterdam and the region can make choices, make investments and allocate responsibilities.

Institutions will have to position themselves anew in relation to these pillars.

Together they form the pillars and the roadmap of the intelligent, caring city. A city in transition, with dilemmas.

sections.title: VI. DILEMMAS

quote.text: The opposite of a profound truth may well be another profound truth.
quote.author: Niels Bohr

sections.bodyMarkdown:
The crossing from a knowledge economy to an intelligence economy is full of collisions.

The question has long since stopped being what we are capable of, and become what we want.

And above all: what are we prepared to lose?

That question rarely gets the room it deserves. Here we put forward a number of dilemmas (out of many) that are going to affect Amsterdam and the region.

None of them has a simple answer. That is precisely the point.

• • •

### Dilemmas

**Rapid progress versus democratic pace**

OpenAI released GPT-4 and within six months hundreds of millions of people were using it. At that moment the European AI Act had already been under negotiation for three years. Technology rewards speed; democracy demands care.

*How much delay is protection, and when does it become standstill?*

**Productivity gains versus fair distribution**

AI can raise productivity by billions. But who captures those gains? In earlier technological revolutions prosperity flowed to owners and investors, while workers had to fight for decades for their share.

*Is work still the right basis for income and solidarity if machines do the work?*

**Mental relief versus thinking capacity**

AI is taking over cognitive tasks. Doctors have diagnoses confirmed by algorithms. Lawyers have contracts screened by software. That saves time and reduces errors. But what happens to our judgement if we practise it less and less?

*How do we preserve crafts and craftsmanship in our society when machines do it better?*

**Safety through data versus freedom of movement**

China's social credit system has measurably reduced crime in certain cities. It has also stripped millions of citizens of the freedom to buy a train ticket. Closer to home: Amsterdam is experimenting with smart cameras that detect nuisance. Every camera makes the city a little safer and a little less free.

*Where is the line between protection and control?*

**Personal assistance versus social isolation**

Replika, an AI companion app, has millions of users who talk to their digital friend every day. For lonely people it offers comfort. But research by the American Psychological Association shows that digital interaction raises the threshold for human contact.

*What happens to our relationships when convenience replaces contact?*

**Universal access versus craftsmanship**

With Midjourney anyone can produce in seconds an illustration that ten years ago took weeks. With GPT anyone can write an essay. Access to creative work has been democratised, and at the same time the distinction between a masterpiece and a decent attempt is blurring.

*Do we want broad access, even if depth becomes rarer?*

**Energy consumption now versus societal breakthroughs later**

Training one large AI model consumes as much electricity as 130 American households in an entire year (IEA, 2025). That same AI optimises energy grids for renewable sources, predicts wildfires, models climate scenarios and helps design new materials for batteries and CO₂ capture.

*Do we accept today's ecological costs as an investment in tomorrow's solutions?*

**Hope of progress versus fear of loss**

The steam engine made handloom weavers redundant. Many ended up in poverty. Generations later, living standards had risen for everyone. The ‘Luddites’ who smashed machines are now seen as short-sighted, but their fear was real and so was their loss.

*Can we acknowledge loss without blocking progress?*

### The Intelligence Assembly

These (and other) dilemmas are too big and too important to leave to engineers, columnists or policymakers alone. They touch the foundations of how we live together.

That is why we propose setting up an **intelligence assembly**: a society-wide citizens' panel that deliberates on the great dilemmas of the intelligence economy. Not a talking shop. A structural part of Amsterdam's decision-making process.

An assembly in which understanding precedes judgement. In which the city does not choose between fear and ambition, but learns to take both seriously. In which vertical maturity becomes practised habit.

• • •

A city and a region that want to grow from a knowledge economy into an intelligence economy need this: a *society-wide conversation*.

A conversation that takes the dilemmas seriously. That gives citizens the room to understand first and judge afterwards.

A dialogue that builds the *vertical maturity* our democracy now needs so badly.

A city with the capacity to bear tension and still choose a direction.

> **From polarisation to direction. Dilemmas bring opportunities and risks together in a single conversation. They do not force consensus, but they do make conscious choices possible.**

sections.title: VII. CHOICES

quote.text: AI enables us to use the gains of the digital revolution to clean up the mess of the industrial revolution.
quote.author: Max Welling

sections.bodyMarkdown:
On the choices that lie ahead: in strategy, in story and in execution.

And on why Amsterdam does not need a positioning but an essence.

So that we can make the conceptual framework concrete and practical for Amsterdam and its region.

• • •

### Strategy

The very patterns that hold us back are the starting point for three strategic lines.

1. **Discovery mode switched on again.** From protection mode to discovery mode. We shift the public conversation from naming risks alone to designing possibilities as well. Not by preaching optimism. Above all by organising (vertical) maturity.  
2. **Building new value, instead of mainly redistributing it.** Builders are given a central role again. Entrepreneurship and technology are explicitly part of our public values. We make room for experiment, correction and learning. Equality of opportunity arises above all from the creation of new value. New broad prosperity.  
3. **Organising scope for action, society-wide.** Critical thinking without perspective leads to paralysis. We translate insight into choices, make systems comprehensible instead of merely problematic, and connect policy, culture and technology into concrete design assignments.

These three lines are the route along which Amsterdam recovers its strategic relevance and earns a place at the table where the rules of the intelligence economy are being written.

### Story

For years now, in Amsterdam's policy rooms and marketing departments, people have been searching for the tech story of Amsterdam. For a slogan, a positioning, a label with which the city can distinguish itself internationally in the age of AI.

But Amsterdam's story does not have to be invented. It is already there. It is our city itself.

Amsterdam was built on water that had to be mastered. On trade that had to be organised. On difference that had to be endured.

This city has never existed by virtue of one idea, one sector or one moral claim.

It existed by virtue of collaboration under pressure. That is the story.

Not a slogan we think up. Above all an essence we activate. And precisely for that reason we should not let ourselves be tempted into a one-dimensional positioning narrative.

The temptation is strong to cast Amsterdam as the city of *responsible AI*, or of *safety-first*, or of *human-centred technology*. Understandable: it fits our self-image and the tone of the European debate. But it is too narrow.

Because Amsterdam is not only the city of ethical reflection. It is the city of both Spinoza and Adyen. Of both the Concertgebouw and Booking.com. Of both PICNIC and fundamental research. Of both carefulness and nerve.

A city that reduces itself to one dimension of AI (i.e. safety, ethics, responsibility, people) makes itself small. It positions itself as the referee in a match that others are playing.

The AI and innovation landscape is broad:

- There is **scientific AI**, fundamental research that generates new knowledge.

- There is **industrial AI**, applications that transform production processes.

- There is **public AI**, systems that improve public services.

- There is **creative AI**, technology that enriches art, media and design.

Amsterdam does not have to choose. Amsterdam can connect it all. That is what this city has always done.

Amsterdam's story in the intelligence economy is not about one claim. It is about the quality of our collaboration. About the ability to let scientists, entrepreneurs, administrators and residents build solutions together that work, technically, economically and socially. The city that shows that you can innovate and include at the same time. Accelerate and anchor. Build and protect.

If we build from that essence, the story comes of its own accord. Not as a marketing campaign, but as a reputation. Not as a slogan.

Amsterdam, a city that is honest about the future, dilemmas included.

### Design requirements and Urban Tech Coalitions (UTCs)

At the core of execution are **Urban Tech Coalitions (UTCs)**: focused, temporary partnerships around concrete urban challenges where technology, entrepreneurship and public delivery come together.

Coalitions with a clear mandate and visible results.

Amsterdam has no shortage of ideas or talent. The city has a shortage of coherence, delivery capacity and scale. UTCs are the answer to that shortage.

They form the link between vision and execution: the place where the five pillars of the intelligence economy become concrete.

To keep coalitions from fragmenting, we apply six knock-out design requirements:

**One. Start with an urgent urban challenge.** Every coalition starts from a concrete, socially recognisable problem where public value is at stake. Not technology in search of a problem, but an issue that is visible to residents, relevant to government and socially urgent. *Without urgency there is no legitimacy.*

*Think of:*

- *Quay walls, bridges, roads: inspection, maintenance, planning, material optimisation*  
- *Grid congestion and delivery pressure: shortage of people, speeding up construction and management*  
- *Waste, circularity and logistics: smarter separation, collection, routing, enforcement*  
- *Municipal services: waiting times, workload, error reduction, better triage*  
- *Safety in public space: situational insight, incident response, order and calm*

**Two. Demand economic weight and scaling potential.** The issue must carry substantial economic weight: in market size, savings potential or social impact. Scaling beyond a single pilot must be possible, preferably with (national or) European reach. Coalitions that cannot scale do not contribute to the strategic relevance of the region. *We are not building niche solutions but points of leverage.*

*Think of:*

- *Energy and grid management: a multi-billion challenge, scalable across the region*  
- *Infrastructure and the engineering chain: engineering firms and public clients*  
- *The port as an export model: from Amsterdam to Rotterdam and Antwerp*  
- *Urban mobility: a larger market than last mile delivery alone*  
- *Healthcare and imaging data: a strong base, broad European demand*

**Three. Require ecosystem depth and an AI knowledge base.** There must be sufficient technological capacity in place to carry scale. That means: available data, relevant startups and scale-ups in the domain, the presence of AI expertise through institutes such as ICAI and Amsterdam AI, availability of talent and a connection to investment flows. *No ecosystem, no coalition.*

*Think of:*

- *Amsterdam AI and UvA VU teams working on image AI, foundation models, world models*  
- *ICAI labs and their coupling to public challenges*  
- *A strong ecosystem in fintech and cyber as a building block for public applications*  
- *Data-rich domains: the built environment, mobility, healthcare and port logistics*  
- *A link to international benchmarks and spin out best practices via Dealroom*

**Four. Connect technology directly to delivery capacity.** Every coalition contains at least one public party with a mandate, one knowledge institution with AI expertise and entrepreneurs from the tech ecosystem. Technology must be directly connected to an implementing organisation, a physical or digital environment, or a concrete launching customer. *Without delivery capacity it remains an experiment.*

*Think of:*

- *The municipality as a client with scale: procurement, policy, delivery, space, CTO line*  
- *Port of Amsterdam as a testing ground with clear boundaries, governance and ownership*  
- *Cooperation with the VNG to translate results to other municipalities*  
- *One lead stakeholder per challenge, to increase openness and limit friction*

**Five. Design for the capacity to learn.** From day one a coalition must be technically repeatable, administratively scalable and economically defensible. It also generates data, publishes insights and improves iteratively. Learning is part of the design, not a by-product. *Pilots without a path to scale do not count.*

*Think of:*

- *Traceable AI as the standard for government use: auditability, explainability, logging*  
- *Sandboxes and low regulation zones for robotics, autonomous shipping, physical tests*  
- *Building in parallel, outside organisational immune systems, integrating into the line organisation later*  
- *City to city programmes via city networks such as Bloomberg leadership*

**Six. Build in trust and public legitimacy explicitly.** Every coalition is transparent, explainable and makes room for public dialogue. Trust is a design requirement, the condition under which technology earns public legitimacy.

*Think of:*

- *City requirements for traceability and accountability to citizens*  
- *Publicly recognisable use cases that show immediate benefit instead of abstract pilots*  
- *Public dialogue tied to real choices, real tests and real outcomes*  
- *Ethical and legal frameworks as an accelerator: clear rules, less noise*  
- *A focus on applications where public values are made measurable*

These six requirements make sure that UTCs do not fragment, do not remain symbolic, do not become purely technological and do not stay purely a matter of policy.

They generate real, scalable building power.

### Selection criteria

The six design requirements determine whether a coalition can work. But Amsterdam has no shortage of initiatives; we have a shortage of focus. That is why we recommend additional weighting criteria for which projects to activate first.

- **Social impact** carries the greatest weight, at 30%. How many citizens and businesses benefit? How much public value does it deliver and how much cost does it save?

- **Economic weight and scalability** counts for 20%. How large is the scaling potential, preferably up to European level? To what extent does it unlock private investment?

- **Ecosystem depth and technological feasibility** weighs 20%. Are the required AI technology, data and relevant parties genuinely available?

- **Delivery capacity** counts for 15%. Are there parties in place that can build, test and roll out now?

- **Trust and legitimacy** weighs 15%. Is the project organised transparently, explainably and inclusively?

If there are more applications than resources, four prioritisation rules apply.

1. **Impact comes before innovation.** Projects that directly solve a large social problem take precedence over initiatives that are technologically interesting but limited in impact.  
2. **Scalable comes before niche.** Projects with regional, national or European scaling potential are ranked higher.  
3. **Rapid visibility counts.** Projects that deliver tangible public value within twelve to twenty-four months take precedence over long-term R&D. That already has a place within NADI.  
4. **Private co-funding weighs in.** The more private investment rides along, the higher the priority.

sections.title: VIII. BUILDING TOGETHER

quote.text: Is this policy, or has it been thought through?
quote.author: Jan Schaefer

sections.bodyMarkdown:
The New Amsterdam Agenda does not present a new action programme or policy programme.

The overwhelming majority of what follows is already sitting on various desks, in national plans, and with knowledge institutions, companies and civil-society organisations.

The core task is to offer a vision, catalyse coalitions and activate what already exists.

Because there is no overarching vision. Coalitions still barely step outside their own bubble. And this moment demands more urgency and speed than we currently see.

The New Amsterdam Agenda has made a start — use it as encouragement to act.

![New Amsterdam Agenda](/assets/03agendanieuwamsterdam.png)

• • •

### Moonshots

We formulate three compelling moonshots that serve as an engine for collaboration. Moonshots are not dreams.

They are design challenges that activate all five pillars and force parties that currently operate in isolation to work together:

**Moonshot 1. Urban Tech Coalitions.** Focused coalitions around *urgent urban challenges* where AI and technology can deliver public value directly.

*Think of AI-driven preventive care by neighbourhood, smart urban logistics, energy optimisation amid grid congestion, or data-driven improvement of municipal services.*

Every coalition satisfies the six design requirements and delivers visible results within two to three years.

Ambition: €250 million in innovation funding available for UTC projects in the region over the next 12 years.

**Moonshot 2. Societal Coalitions.** Urban Tech Coalitions built around the *broader societal conditions* for the intelligence economy.

- First ambition: make 100,000 Amsterdam residents AI-literate, from primary school to the boardroom. Not only technically, but also in navigating the (moral) dilemmas this technology raises.

- Second ambition: an intelligence assembly in which 1,000 Amsterdam residents help think through the dilemmas of the transition on a structural basis.

**Moonshot 3. NADI in Amsterdam.** Amsterdam positions itself as the host city for the National Agency for Disruptive Innovation. The combination of AI research, startup ecosystem, data-centre capacity and urban living labs makes the city the logical home base.

### Getting started right away: government as co-builder

Five actions that create immediate momentum:

1. **Train administrators:** technological leadership begins with technological understanding.  
2. **Reorient institutions:** most are still organised around the knowledge economy.  
3. **Translate national to local:** map the Wennink Report and AI Delta Plan onto pillars and coalitions.  
4. **Install a Digital Infrastructure Board:** strategic governance of digital infrastructure.  
5. **Launch the first UTC:** one challenge, one coalition, two years, a visible result.

### The five pillars and their measures

**Pillar 1: Physical foundation, compute as a utility, sovereignty**

- Urban infrastructure vision: A vision for the physical digital foundation

- Digital Infrastructure Board: Strategic governance of infrastructure

- Compute for societal challenges: Compute as a public utility

- Narrative campaign: Compute as a prerequisite for solutions.

**Pillar 2: Collective capability, public good, access for everyone**

- Trusted Data Spaces: Secure sharing of urban data

- Municipality as launching customer: Government as first customer

- SME & neighbourhood-based AI Labs: AI access for everyone

- AI literacy as a basic provision: teaching 100,000 residents to work with AI

**Pillar 3: Ambition, ecosystem stewardship, conditions for entrepreneurship**

- NADI: Bringing the National Agency for Disruptive Innovation to Amsterdam

- Ecosystem stewardship: Coherent direction for the ecosystem

- Builders' priority lane: A fast track and enabling conditions for scale-ups

- AI Talent programme: Attracting and retaining top talent

- Students as builders: Students building the city

- Accelerated valorisation & spin-outs: Getting knowledge to market faster

- Dutch ELLIS Institute: National AI Research Centre

- International narrative & advocacy: Making Amsterdam visible on the world stage

**Pillar 4: Choices, connecting technology to values, room to experiment**

- Amsterdam AI compass: A moral framework for applying AI

- Amsterdam as a living lab: The city as a test environment

- Sandbox programme: Safe experimentation with AI

- Government as launching customer: Public demand as a flywheel

- Focus on applied AI: Solutions to real problems

**Pillar 5: Trust as a factor of production, transparency, legitimacy**

- Societal dialogue: A broad conversation about the transition and its dilemmas

- Urban/regional trust framework: Ground rules for AI use

- Public trust layers: Transparent AI infrastructure

- Living labs for responsible AI: Testing with public values

Government is shifting from assessor to co-builder — by building public values into the design requirements, but above all by organising the enabling conditions.

### National plans, local action

The New Amsterdam Agenda does not stand alone. It builds on three national plans: the Wennink Report as an economic compass, the National AI Delta Plan as an implementation framework, and the AI Deep Dive Report for focus and application.

What these plans have in common is that they set direction but leave their translation to the urban and regional level open.

New Amsterdam brings these national threads together into one coherent urban logic. We have applied the measures from these reports locally and allocated them across the pillars of the intelligence economy.

### Flywheel

The five pillars of the intelligence economy are mutually dependent.

Energy and computing power make AI applications possible. Data and access determine who can take part. Entrepreneurship and talent provide application and scale. Compass and laboratories provide direction and learning. Trust infrastructure secures legitimacy and public support.

Choices in one pillar accelerate the others. Investing in compute makes data sharing worthwhile. Data sharing makes entrepreneurship possible. Entrepreneurship creates visible applications. Visible applications build trust. Trust makes further investment politically feasible. That is the flywheel of the intelligent city. And it begins with the first choice.

### The future coalition

The intelligence economy is coming. The question is whether Amsterdam becomes a co-designer or a spectator.

Picture Amsterdam in 2038:

- **Equal digital opportunity:** a city where innovation is accessible to every resident and entrepreneur, so that no one falls into a technological disadvantage.  
- **A thriving tech & AI ecosystem:** a city where one of Europe's strongest innovation communities does not operate alongside society but is inseparably part of it, making its progress felt in every neighbourhood, every sector and every generation.  
- **A future-ready generation:** a place where children grow up with abundant self-confidence and know exactly how to use smart technology for their own development.  
- **A healthy and liveable environment:** a clean city with seamless transport, affordable green power and rapid access to high-quality care.  
- **Technology in service of people:** a safe living environment in which government ensures that human values and privacy always come first.  
- **A close-knit and engaged community:** a city where progress is widely supported, because innovations have been developed in full transparency and together with residents.

That Amsterdam does not exist yet. But it can exist. If we start now, and if we do it together.

That calls for a coalition bigger than politics and more concrete than a set of separate networks.

A future coalition that brings the municipality and delivery organisations together with education, healthcare, housing corporations, entrepreneurs from startups to corporates, grid operators, cultural institutions, and residents and neighbourhood networks.

Everyone keeps their role and their stake. No one operates apart from the whole any longer.

### Building Together

New Amsterdam is a temporary, decentralised initiative that serves.

We provide direction, connect parties and catalyse coalitions.

Ownership and execution lie where they belong: with the institutions, organisations and people who actually build.

That is precisely why this is an open invitation: to actively broaden the conversation to perspectives beyond the circle in which this agenda originated.

The effort aligns with recent national and European frameworks and reinforces them at the urban and regional level.

At the same time, the agenda builds on the many initiatives already under way in and around Amsterdam. In this way it connects national ambition with local strength, and separate initiatives with a shared direction.

In 2038 we will dissolve ourselves. By then the city must be mature enough to carry this way of thinking and building forward on its own.

Spinoza began with understanding. We end with building. That is the movement of this essay, and its invitation to the city.

• • •

**Will you help build it?**

Ideas, feedback, or want to get involved? Send a message to [rubenswindow@gmail.com](mailto:rubenswindow@gmail.com)

sections.title: EPILOGUE: A NEW CROSSING

quote.text: The more we understand a thing, the more or the better we love it. (Amor erga Deum est ipsa mentis Dei amor, quo Deus se ipsum amat)
quote.author: Spinoza, Ethics V, Proposition 20

sections.bodyMarkdown:
In the seventeenth century, the Netherlands had the best transport system in the world.

The network of horse-drawn barges connected all the major cities of the Republic (Amsterdam, Haarlem, Leiden, Delft, Rotterdam, Utrecht) with a precision and regularity that amazed travellers from across Europe. Fixed departure times. Fixed fares. Comfortable boats, drawn by horses along dedicated canals dug for the purpose. An Englishman who made the crossing from Amsterdam to Haarlem in 1640 wrote home in astonishment: nowhere in Europe could one travel so quickly, cheaply and pleasantly.

It was no accident. It was the product of generations of collaboration among cities, water authorities, entrepreneurs and governments. *Potentia*, Spinoza would say. Power with one another, not over one another.

And it worked so well that no one wanted to tamper with it.

• • •

When the steam train arrived in Europe (first in England in 1825, then in Belgium in 1835), Dutch public administrators, merchants and experts debated for years whether such an invention was really needed here. The horse-drawn barge worked perfectly well, didn’t it? The network functioned, didn’t it? The horses knew the route.

It was not until 1839, years later than neighbouring countries, that the first steam train ran in the Netherlands: from Amsterdam to Haarlem, along exactly the same route the horse-drawn barge had served for two centuries.

It is a gentle story, but the mechanism is the same as with the entrepôt system. Whoever has the best system is the last to change it. Those accustomed to a world that works are the slowest to see that the rules are changing.

Not out of stupidity. Seldom out of ill will. But because success breeds its own blindness.

• • •

Spinoza knew this.

What paralyses people and communities, he wrote, is not change itself. It is the unwillingness to understand it. Those who do not understand what is in motion are moved by it. Those who do not shape are shaped.

But Spinoza never stopped at the diagnosis. Alongside the passive affects, he placed the active ones.

And the most powerful of these he called *amor intellectualis*: intellectual love. Not sentiment, not romance, but the deep connection that arises when people understand together what is truly happening. When they look reality straight in the eye and then decide together what to make of it.

For him, that love is not a private matter. It is a political force. The architecture of a society that does not paralyse itself, but strengthens itself. A path to the intelligent, caring city.

“*Nothing is more useful to man than man*,” he wrote, as a political reality. Communities that collaborate from a place of understanding are more powerful than communities that collaborate from distrust.

• • •

Amsterdam once again faces a crossing.

Not by horse-drawn barge. But the question is the same as ever: do we understand what is in motion, and are we prepared to build the next infrastructure together before others do it for us?

The knowledge economy was our horse-drawn barge. Excellent. Proven. A source of pride. And just as then, the temptation is strong to say: it works, doesn’t it? The network functions, doesn’t it?

But the intelligence economy requires different infrastructure. Different rules. Different forms of collaboration. And above all: the capacity to act—not waiting for the new reality to befall us, but helping to design it.

Spinoza was banished by a community that understood what he thought but feared the consequences. He left, ground his lenses and wrote his philosophy in silence. But he continued to believe.

• • •

This essay began with a man who was banished from Amsterdam because his ideas were too uncomfortable.

It ends with an invitation to that same city.

To do what he proposed: understand what is truly happening, transform passive affects into active ones, and from that strength build together what does not yet exist.

**Will you help build it?**

• • •

The New Amsterdam Agenda is emphatically a point of departure, not a final report. It is an open invitation to think and build together, and to actively broaden the conversation to include perspectives beyond the circle in which this agenda originated.
